pack.name: Starter · Modern Workplace
pack.description: 15 diplomatic Slack, meeting, and alignment phrases without stiff corporate jargon.

items.flat: I want to inform you in advance about a potential problem with next week's deadline.
items.upgraded: Just flagging this early—the API integration might slip by a couple of days.

lines.speaker: Dev
lines.text: Quick heads-up: flagging this early so nobody's surprised—vendor review is taking longer than expected.

lines.speaker: PM
lines.text: Super helpful, thanks for the early heads-up. Let's adjust the buffer.

lines.speaker: Designer
lines.text: I wanted to flag a potential bottleneck on mobile assets before we lock scope.

lines.speaker: Lead
lines.text: Glad you brought it up now while we still have wiggle room.

items.nuance: One of the highest-trust habits in modern tech and product teams. 'Flagging' sounds proactive and collaborative, whereas 'warning you' or 'reporting an issue' can sound stiff or alarmist.
items.polish: zasygnalizować coś zawczasu / dać wcześnie znać o potencjalnym temacie
items.clozeSentence: Wanted to ___ this early: if legal doesn't sign off by Thursday, we'll need to push the campaign.
items.clozeHint: 4-letter verb meaning to raise a helpful early signal.
items.quizPrompt: I am writing to notify you prematurely regarding a possible schedule delay.
quizOptions: Just flagging this early so we have time to adjust—we might see a two-day slip.
I am submitting an early warning notification of temporal slippage.
I want to wave a red cloth early about the schedule.
I am flagging to you early about a delay.
quizExplanations: Calm, proactive, and sounds like a seasoned product/ops teammate.
'Flag' takes a direct object ('flag this', 'flag a risk'), not 'flag to someone'.
items.sandboxPrompt: Write a short Slack message letting your team know early that a client might ask for extra revisions next week.
items.sandboxSample: Just flagging this early—based on yesterday's sync, the client will likely ask for another round of copy tweaks next week.

items.flat: We should politely disagree with their request to add three new features before Friday.
items.upgraded: I think we need to push back on adding new scope this close to launch.

lines.speaker: PM
lines.text: Sales wants custom reporting included in v1.

lines.speaker: Eng Lead
lines.text: I'd gently push back on that—it'll delay the core release by two weeks.

lines.speaker: Manager
lines.text: You don't have to say yes to every last-minute deck request.

lines.speaker: Analyst
lines.text: Fair point—I'll push back on timelines when I'm already at capacity.

items.nuance: Essential modern workplace phrasing for constructive disagreement or boundary-setting. Often softened with 'gently' ('I'd gently push back on...') so you sound collaborative rather than combative.
items.polish: postawić granicę / grzecznie zakwestionować / nie zgodzić się bezrefleksyjnie
items.clozeSentence: If the client asks for free weekend support, don't hesitate to push ___ on that.
items.quizPrompt: We must refuse their unrealistic deadline and propose a more sustainable timeline.
quizOptions: We should push back on that timeline and propose something realistic for the team.
We must combat their unrealistic deadline aggressively.
We need to push behind their deadline proposal.
We should push back their deadline.
quizExplanations: Constructive, firm, and standard across modern workplaces.
Needs preposition 'on' ('push back on that timeline').
items.sandboxPrompt: Suggest to a colleague that your team should diplomatically resist a stakeholder's last-minute request.
items.sandboxSample: I'd gently push back on squeezing another survey in before Friday—we won't have time to analyze the data properly.
sandboxRubric: Cadence: Includes a brief, logical rationale.

items.flat: Let's quickly review these numbers together to make sure we haven't made an obvious mistake.
items.upgraded: Before we send this to the client, let's sanity-check the pricing table.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Got two minutes to sanity-check my assumptions on the Q3 forecast?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Sure, drop the sheet link—happy to give it a quick look.

lines.speaker: Kira
lines.text: Let's sanity-check this flow with two support agents before we build it.

lines.speaker: PM
lines.text: Smart call—they'll spot edge cases right away.

items.nuance: Warm, collaborative phrasing that frames a review as a quick common-sense verification rather than a formal audit or interrogation.
items.polish: sprawdźmy to na zdrowy rozsądek / rzućmy okiem, czy to się trzyma kupy
items.clozeSentence: Can you sanity-___ this email draft for me? I want to make sure the tone lands right.
items.quizPrompt: Could you quickly verify my logic here to ensure it makes basic practical sense?
quizOptions: Mind sanity-checking my logic here for two minutes?
Could you verify my mental health regarding this logic?
Please conduct a preliminary rationality audit on my reasoning.
Could you sanity-test my mind on this?
quizExplanations: Casual, collegial, and completely natural in modern offices.
items.sandboxPrompt: Ask a teammate on Slack to quickly look over a proposal or timeline before you share it wider.
items.sandboxSample: Hey! Got a sec to sanity-check this rollout timeline before I post it in #general?
sandboxRubric: Collocation: Used 'sanity-check' as a verb or noun naturally.

items.flat: We should include Sarah in this email thread so she stays informed about our decision.
items.upgraded: Let's loop Sarah in now so she's not caught off guard next week.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: Looping in @Priya from Design so she has context on the new onboarding copy.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Thanks for looping me in! Reviewing the doc now.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Who else needs to sign off on the vendor contract?

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: We should probably loop Finance in early before we negotiate payment terms.

items.nuance: Standard, friendly workplace verb for adding someone to a conversation, thread, or decision. Much smoother and warmer than 'include in the correspondence'.
items.polish: włączyć kogoś w temat / dodać do wątku / trzymać na bieżąco
items.clozeSentence: Once we narrow down the shortlist, let's loop the hiring manager ___.
items.quizPrompt: I am adding David to this conversation because he handles European logistics.
quizOptions: Looping David in here since he oversees European logistics.
Circling David inside this correspondence for European logistics.
Incorporating David into the communicative circuit.
Looping David on here for European logistics.
quizExplanations: Crisp, natural email/Slack phrasing used every single day.
Distorts the metaphor ('loop in', not 'circle inside').
items.sandboxPrompt: Write a quick line adding a teammate from legal or design into an ongoing Slack or email thread.
items.sandboxSample: Looping @Marta in so she can weigh in on the privacy wording before we publish.
sandboxRubric: Register: Clear, collaborative async communication style.
Cadence: States briefly why they're being added.

items.flat: I do not have enough time or mental energy to take on another project this week.
items.upgraded: I'd love to help, but I honestly don't have the bandwidth for another deck right now.

lines.speaker: Lead
lines.text: Any chance you could lead the Q2 workshop prep?

lines.speaker: Analyst
lines.text: I don't have the bandwidth this week with the audit, though I could pick it up next Wednesday.

lines.speaker: PM
lines.text: Does Design have bandwidth for a quick landing page refresh?

lines.speaker: Design Lead
lines.text: Pretty tight until Friday—next sprint is wide open.

items.nuance: A polite, professional way to say 'I'm maxed out' without sounding overwhelmed or complaining. Frames your time as a finite capacity rather than a personal refusal.
items.polish: mieć moce przerobowe / przestrzeń czasową na coś
items.clozeSentence: I'm swamped through Thursday, so I won't have the ___ to review the draft until Friday.
items.clozeHint: 9-letter tech-derived noun meaning time and mental capacity.
items.quizPrompt: I am too busy with current deadlines to take on an extra side project this month.
quizOptions: I'm at full capacity right now and don't have the bandwidth for another side project.
My internet connection speed is insufficient for another side project.
I suffer from a severe deficit of temporal allocation capacity.
I don't have bandwidths for another project.
quizExplanations: Polite, professional boundary-setting used across modern workplaces.
Literal tech meaning rather than workplace capacity.
items.sandboxPrompt: Politely tell a teammate you can't take on an extra task today, while offering when you'll be free.
items.sandboxSample: I don't have the bandwidth to dig into this today, but I can block an hour for it tomorrow morning.
sandboxRubric: Register: Calm, professional boundary without sounding stressed.
Collocation: Used 'have the bandwidth for / to [verb]' accurately.
Cadence: Offers a realistic alternative time.

items.flat: Let's pause this topic and come back to it later when we have more information.
items.upgraded: Let's table this for now and revisit it once we see the user survey results.

lines.speaker: PM (NY)
lines.text: We've spent twenty minutes debating icon styles and still haven't covered launch risks.

lines.speaker: Lead (SF)
lines.text: Agreed—let's table this for now and pick it up async in Figma.

lines.speaker: London Lead
lines.text: Quick note: in UK English 'table a proposal' means bring it onto the table right now, whereas in the US it means postpone it!

lines.speaker: NY PM
lines.text: Good catch—saying 'let's table this for now and revisit Thursday' makes it 100% clear on both sides.

items.nuance: CRITICAL US vs. UK OPPOSITE: In US English, 'to table something' means to postpone/shelve it; in UK parliamentary & business English, 'to table something' means to put it on the agenda for immediate discussion! Always add 'for now' or 'until Thursday' on international calls to avoid complete misunderstanding.
items.polish: odłóżmy ten temat na później (US) / zgłosić pod obrady (tradycyjny UK)
items.clozeSentence: Since we're short on time, let's ___ this discussion until Thursday's sync.
items.clozeHint: 5-letter verb meaning postpone/shelve in US workplace English.
items.quizPrompt: You want to pause a side-debate in a meeting with both US and UK teammates without confusion.
quizOptions: Let's table this for now and revisit it on Thursday once we have the data.
Let's table this immediately so we discuss it next month.
Let us desk this conversational tangent until a subsequent assembly.
Let's put this on the table so we ignore it today.
quizExplanations: Adding 'for now' and 'revisit it on Thursday' makes the postponement crystal clear across both US and UK English.
Contradictory ('immediately' vs 'next month') and triggers the US/UK opposite-meaning trap.
Confuses the literal UK sense with postponement.
items.sandboxPrompt: Politely pause a topic during a meeting that's running over time so the group can finish the main agenda.
items.sandboxSample: That's a great point, though with five minutes left, let's table this for now and pick it up first thing Monday.
sandboxRubric: Collocation: Included a time cue ('for now', 'until Monday') to eliminate US/UK ambiguity.

items.flat: We need to have a short meeting so everyone agrees on the main goals before starting.
items.upgraded: Let's jump on a quick 15-minute call to get aligned on priorities before kickoff.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Before Engineering starts scoping, let's make sure we're aligned on what 'done' looks like.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: 100%—I'll drop a short bullet summary so we can get aligned fast.

lines.speaker: Marketing
lines.text: Are we aligned on the launch date?

lines.speaker: Product
lines.text: Yep, locked for the 18th.

items.nuance: Much lighter and more natural than 'reach consensus' or 'harmonize our objectives'. 'Get aligned on' focuses on shared practical clarity rather than forcing total agreement on every detail.
items.polish: uzgodnić wspólne stanowisko / zgrać się co do (celów, priorytetów)
items.clozeSentence: We don't need a huge deck—just a quick chat to get ___ on next steps.
items.quizPrompt: Let's make sure Marketing and Sales agree on the messaging before we send the email.
quizOptions: Let's make sure Marketing and Sales are aligned on the messaging before it goes out.
Let's make sure Marketing and Sales are lined up straight on the messaging.
Let us achieve symmetrical ideological alignment prior to dispatch.
Let's get aligned with the messaging together.
quizExplanations: Clean, natural, and conversational modern workplace English.
Literal distortion ('lined up' means standing in a physical queue).
Collocates with 'on' ('aligned on [topic]'), 'with' is used for people ('aligned with Sarah').
items.sandboxPrompt: Suggest a brief check-in with a teammate so you both agree on priorities for the week.
items.sandboxSample: Got ten minutes after lunch to get aligned on our top three priorities for this sprint?

items.flat: If we choose the faster option, what negative consequence or disadvantage will we have to accept?
items.upgraded: Shipping by Friday sounds great, but what's the trade-off here—are we skipping QA?

lines.speaker: Tech Lead
lines.text: We can use the third-party widget and launch twice as fast.

lines.speaker: PM
lines.text: Nice—what's the trade-off? Less customization down the road?

lines.speaker: Ops
lines.text: Switching to annual billing saves 20%.

lines.speaker: Founder
lines.text: What's the trade-off—strict lock-in if our team size changes?

items.nuance: One of the sharpest questions you can ask in any strategic or product conversation. Shows mature systems thinking—recognizing that every choice balances competing upside and downside.
items.polish: jaki jest tu kompromis / co poświęcamy w zamian?
items.clozeSentence: Lower upfront cost is tempting, so what's the ___—longer lead times?
items.clozeHint: Hyphenated noun meaning a balance between two competing qualities.
items.quizPrompt: If we pick the cheaper supplier, what disadvantage do we accept in exchange?
quizOptions: If we go with the cheaper supplier, what's the trade-off—slower shipping or lower quality?
If we go with the cheaper supplier, what is the exchange punishment?
What negative counter-variables accompany this procurement selection?
What's the trade-in here with the cheaper supplier?
quizExplanations: Sharp, pragmatic, and completely natural in everyday and business speech.
'Trade-in' refers to exchanging an old phone/car for credit, not strategic compromises.
items.sandboxPrompt: Ask a teammate what downside comes with choosing a faster or cheaper approach on a project.
items.sandboxSample: Building it in-house gives us full control, though what's the trade-off—two extra weeks of dev time?
sandboxRubric: Cadence: Connects two competing priorities clearly.

items.flat: When you simplify all the details, the core issue is really just a lack of clear ownership.
items.upgraded: At the end of the day, it really boils down to whether users trust the data.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: We've been debating five different tools all afternoon.

lines.speaker: Kira
lines.text: Honestly, it boils down to two things: price and how fast the team can learn it.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Why did they pick our competitor?

lines.speaker: Clara
lines.text: Boiled down to a single missing integration.

items.nuance: A vivid culinary metaphor (reducing a sauce to its essence) used effortlessly in both casual and executive conversations to cut through noise and name the core factor.
items.clozeSentence: You can analyze ten metrics, but retention usually boils ___ to how good the first five minutes feel.
items.quizPrompt: In essence, the whole disagreement is simply about budget priority.
quizOptions: Basically, the whole disagreement boils down to budget priorities.
Basically, the whole disagreement cooks down to budget priorities.
Fundamentally, the dispute distills into fiscal prioritization.
The disagreement boils up to budget priorities.
quizExplanations: Wrong verb ('boils down to', never 'cooks down to').
items.sandboxPrompt: Summarize a complex choice or problem down to its single most important factor.
items.sandboxSample: For most remote teams, good async communication really boils down to writing clear updates.
sandboxRubric: Collocation: Used 'boils down to + noun/clause' accurately.

items.flat: I haven't made a final decision yet, but currently I prefer Option B.
items.upgraded: I'm leaning toward Option B, though I'm open to hearing if anyone sees a flaw.

lines.speaker: PM
lines.text: Thursday morning or Friday afternoon for the live demo?

lines.speaker: Designer
lines.text: I'm leaning toward Thursday morning while everyone's energy is fresh.

lines.speaker: Lead
lines.text: Where are you landing on the two finalists?

lines.speaker: Engineer
lines.text: Leaning toward Maya—her systems thinking stood out.

items.nuance: Signals a clear preference while remaining collaborative and open to input—ideal when nudging a decision forward without shutting down discussion.
items.clozeSentence: Between the two layouts, I'm leaning ___ the cleaner single-column version.
items.quizPrompt: My current preference is to keep the pricing simple, though I am open to other ideas.
quizOptions: I'm leaning toward keeping the pricing simple, though I'm open to other takes.
I am tilting physically in the direction of simple pricing.
My provisional inclination gravitates toward pricing simplicity.
I'm leaning to keep the pricing simple.
items.sandboxPrompt: State which option you currently favor for a team decision while inviting feedback.
items.sandboxSample: I'm leaning toward launching with a small beta group first so we can iron out bugs quietly.
sandboxRubric: Cadence: Includes a brief reason or openness cue.

items.flat: We agree on the main plan, and now we just need to resolve a few small remaining issues.
items.upgraded: The main terms look solid—we just need to iron out a few details on onboarding.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.text: How did the call with the Berlin partner go?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Really well! We agreed on scope and just need to iron out the billing details tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Is the venue locked in?

lines.speaker: Chloe
lines.text: Yep, just ironing out the final catering numbers with them.

items.nuance: Like smoothing wrinkles out of a shirt—used when the big picture is agreed upon and only minor practical wrinkles remain. Also works as 'iron out the kinks' (for early bugs/glitches).
items.clozeSentence: Once we iron ___ the schedule with Legal, we'll be ready to announce the date.
items.quizPrompt: The big picture is agreed upon; we only have to fix a few minor logistical points.
quizOptions: We're aligned on the big picture—just need to iron out a few logistical details.
We're aligned on the big picture—just need to press flat the logistics.
Macro-alignment is complete; minor logistical smoothing remains.
We just need to iron up a few details.
quizExplanations: Natural, optimistic, and standard workplace English.
items.sandboxPrompt: Tell a teammate that the main concept is approved and you just need a quick call to finalize small details.
items.sandboxSample: Great news—Leadership signed off on the concept, so let's hop on a call to iron out the launch details.
sandboxRubric: Collocation: Used 'iron out [the details / a few kinks]' cleanly.

items.flat: Let's stop discussing this specific technical detail in the big group meeting and talk about it separately later.
items.upgraded: Since this only affects two teams, let's take it offline so we don't hold everyone up.

lines.speaker: Engineer
lines.text: Should we dive into the database migration script right now?

lines.speaker: Tech Lead
lines.text: Let's take that offline right after this call so the rest of the group gets time back.

lines.speaker: PM
lines.text: Good catch on that edge case—let's take it offline in a quick DM so we don't clutter this thread.

lines.speaker: QA
lines.text: Sounds good, messaging you now.

items.nuance: In modern remote work, 'taking something offline' doesn't mean turning off Wi-Fi—it simply means moving a niche sub-discussion out of a large meeting or public channel into a smaller 1:1 chat.
items.polish: przegadać to osobno (poza głównym spotkaniem / na boku)
items.clozeSentence: That's a great deep-dive question—let's take it ___ after the all-hands so we stay on schedule.
items.clozeHint: 7-letter compound word meaning outside the main group meeting.
items.quizPrompt: Let's discuss this niche billing edge case separately later instead of keeping twelve people on the call.
quizOptions: Let's take this billing edge case offline so we don't keep the whole group.
Let us disconnect from the internet to discuss this billing edge case.
We should sideline this billing anomaly to a non-networked venue.
Let's put this edge case offline from us.
quizExplanations: Respectful of everyone's time and completely natural in modern meetings.
items.sandboxPrompt: Politely redirect a detailed technical back-and-forth during a group call so the meeting finishes on time.
items.sandboxSample: Let's take the API schema details offline right after this—Alex and I can sync for ten minutes and share the summary.
sandboxRubric: Cadence: Explains briefly why or who will follow up.

items.speechText: a ballpark figure. a rough sense
items.flat: I don't need an exact calculation yet, just an approximate estimate of the cost.
items.upgraded: I don't need exact quotes yet—just a ballpark figure so we know what we're dealing with.

lines.speaker: Founder
lines.text: Any rough sense of what localization for five languages will run us?

lines.speaker: Ops Lead
lines.text: Ballpark figure, probably around $12k–$15k, though I'll get firm quotes tomorrow.

lines.speaker: PM
lines.text: Are we talking two days or two weeks for this refactor?

lines.speaker: Dev
lines.text: Just to give you a rough sense, probably closer to a week.

items.nuance: 'Ballpark figure' (or 'in the ballpark') comes from baseball but is universally understood across US and UK business English. 'A rough sense' is slightly softer and works great for timelines, effort, or sentiment.
items.clozeSentence: We're not locking budgets today—just looking for a ___ figure to see if it's feasible.
items.quizPrompt: Can you give me an approximate estimate of how many hours this redesign will take?
quizOptions: Can you give me a rough sense—or a ballpark figure—of the hours involved?
Can you give me a stadium number of the hours involved?
Please furnish an uncalibrated numerical approximation of labor hours.
Can you give me a ballpark of the hours?
quizExplanations: Natural, low-pressure way to ask for an early estimate without demanding false precision.
items.sandboxPrompt: Ask a teammate or contractor for an approximate cost or timeline estimate before doing detailed scoping.
items.sandboxSample: No need to build a full spreadsheet yet—just looking for a ballpark figure so we can plan Q3.
sandboxRubric: Collocation: Used 'ballpark figure' or 'rough sense' naturally.
Cadence: Reassures the listener that exact precision isn't required yet.

items.flat: Let's focus specifically on the onboarding drop-off rate rather than looking at all metrics at once.
items.upgraded: If we zoom in on mobile sign-ups, that's where almost all the drop-off happens.

lines.speaker: Analyst
lines.text: Overall conversion looks flat, but when you zoom in on returning users, retention jumped 14%.

lines.speaker: PM
lines.text: Whoa, that changes the whole story.

lines.speaker: Lead
lines.text: Let's zoom out for a second on the yearly goal, then zoom in on what needs to happen this month.

lines.speaker: Designer
lines.text: Love that framing.

items.nuance: Paired naturally with 'zoom out' (step back to see the big picture). Much more dynamic and visual than repeating 'focus on' or 'concentrate on'.
items.polish: przyjrzeć się z bliska / skupić się na konkretnym wycinku
items.clozeSentence: Let's zoom ___ on Q4 churn first, since that's our biggest lever right now.
items.quizPrompt: Let's look closely at the specific segment where customer complaints increased.
quizOptions: Let's zoom in on the enterprise segment—that's where support tickets spiked.
Let's magnify our optical lens onto the enterprise segment.
Let us focus our analytical microscope exclusively upon said segment.
Let's zoom onto the enterprise segment.
quizExplanations: Crisp, visual, and completely natural in modern data/product discussions.
items.sandboxPrompt: Direct your team's attention to one specific area of a project or dataset that matters most right now.
items.sandboxSample: Before we touch the homepage, let's zoom in on the checkout step where users are abandoning their carts.
sandboxRubric: Cadence: Connects the specific focus to a clear insight.

items.flat: Debating which office chairs to buy no longer matters because we decided to stay fully remote.
items.upgraded: Honestly, it's a moot point now—the client already signed with another vendor.

lines.speaker: Dev
lines.text: Should we still optimize the legacy checkout flow?

lines.speaker: PM
lines.text: It's a moot point—we're retiring that entire codebase next Friday.

lines.speaker: UK Counsel
lines.text: In traditional UK English, 'a moot point' means a point still open to debate, though most international tech teams use it the US way ('no longer relevant').

lines.speaker: Lead
lines.text: Good to keep in mind on London calls!

items.nuance: TWO KEY TRAPS: (1) Spelling: always 'm-o-o-t', NEVER 'mute point'. (2) US vs. UK nuance: in US and global tech English, 'a moot point' means 'irrelevant / purely academic because events already decided it'; in traditional UK English, it can still mean 'an unresolved point open to debate'.
items.polish: kwestia bezprzedmiotowa (US) / kwestia sporna, otwarta do dyskusji (tradycyjny UK)
items.clozeSentence: Since the event got canceled this morning, arguing about catering is a ___ point.
items.quizPrompt: Whether we should have hired an external agency doesn't matter anymore because the campaign is over.
quizOptions: Debating whether to hire an agency is a moot point now—the campaign wrapped yesterday.
Debating whether to hire an agency is a mute point now.
Debating agency engagement is now temporally irrelevant.
Debating whether to hire an agency is a mood point now.
quizExplanations: Correct spelling ('moot') and crisp, natural workplace usage.
Classic spelling trap ('mute' means silent, not 'moot').
items.sandboxPrompt: Point out calmly that a debate is no longer relevant because an outside decision already settled it.
items.sandboxSample: Whether we prefer Thursday or Friday is a moot point now—the speaker is only in town on Wednesday.
sandboxRubric: Cadence: Briefly states the fact that made the debate irrelevant.
